docs.name: 01_Fiji_Mere_FICTIONAL.txt
docs.content:
FICTIONAL TRAINING INTERVIEW — NOT REAL RESEARCH DATA
Participant alias: Mere
Setting: Fictional coastal settlement on Viti Levu, Fiji
Interview language: English; scripted in English, not translated
All people, experiences, events and quotations below are invented.

Interviewer — Q1: Please tell me about your household and an ordinary day here.
Mere: I sell fish at the roadside and grow vegetables behind our house. My mother lives with us, and my two children attend the nearby school. In the afternoon I usually check on a neighbour before preparing food. This shore is where I learned to fish with my father. Our work, family visits and church activities fit together here, so an ordinary day is also a day of looking after people.

Interviewer — Q2: Describe a recent weather or environmental event that disrupted your life.
Mere: During the storm in this fictional interview, the wind began before sunset and the sea came over the road later that night. We moved the children upstairs at my cousin's house. In the morning our cooking shelter had lost its roof and the garden was covered with sand. The sea did not reach every house equally. Two houses farther inland stayed dry, which made the damage feel very uneven.

Interviewer — Q3: How did the event affect drinking water, sanitation, electricity or access to care?
Mere: Our rainwater tank survived, but dirty water entered the pipe connection. We boiled what we could while the power was out, and then shared water from a neighbour's covered tank. I made several trips carrying containers because my mother could not walk that distance. By the third day, collecting water took the hours I normally used to sell fish. A working tank matters, but so does being able to reach it.

Interviewer — Q4: What changed in your work, food supply, income or debts?
Mere: The boats stayed ashore and the roadside stalls were closed. I borrowed money to replace the cooking pots, and we ate the food we had saved for selling. When visitors returned, the catch was smaller and fuel cost more than I could manage. We did not lose only one week of income. We also lost the small reserve that usually helps us through the next difficult week.

Interviewer — Q5: How do you hear about danger, and how do you decide which information to trust?
Mere: The warning came by radio and then a youth volunteer walked from house to house. I trusted the volunteer because she explained when the road might flood and where to go. A message on a phone is useful only when the phone has charge and the words make sense. My mother heard the radio announcement but needed someone to explain the timing slowly. The same warning needed different ways of reaching people.

Interviewer — Q6: Tell me about deciding whether to leave or stay during an emergency.
Mere: The shelter was open, but I worried about leaving my mother's medicines and the fishing gear behind. The path was already wet when we decided to go. My cousin arrived with a cart, so we took the medicines, bedding and children together. We were fortunate to have that help. I would like evacuation planning to include people who cannot move quickly, rather than assuming everyone can carry a bag and walk.

Interviewer — Q7: Who helped, and what did neighbours or community groups do?
Mere: Neighbours cooked together beside the houses that still had roofs. One family shared water, another lent tools, and the youth group cleared fallen branches. That made us feel less alone. But the family renting a room near the landing place was not on the usual household list. They received food later than others. Knowing your neighbours helps, yet a support system should not depend entirely on being well known.

Interviewer — Q8: Did the disruption affect some people more than others?
Mere: I looked after my mother while repairing the stall, so my working day became longer even though my earnings became smaller. My brother helped with the roof, but he returned to his job after two days. People called us resilient, and I appreciated their kindness, but the extra care work stayed with me. Being able to continue does not mean the burden is light or shared equally.

Interviewer — Q9: What support did you receive, and how much say did residents have in decisions?
Mere: Emergency supplies arrived through a local committee. The first distribution was quick, but I did not know how the repair list was decided. Women who sold food asked to attend the planning meeting; it was held at the same time as the market. I do not think the organisers intended to exclude us. Still, a meeting is not open to everyone if attending means losing that day's income.

Interviewer — Q10: What have you changed to prepare for the next disruption?
Mere: We raised the tank connection and keep a sealed box for medicines and documents. The youth group practises checking on older residents. These are changes we can manage ourselves. Raising the whole house would cost much more than we earn. I also worry that a stronger wall at one property could send water towards another. Preparation should look at the whole neighbourhood, not just at the safest single house.

Interviewer — Q11: Have you considered moving away, temporarily or permanently?
Mere: My sister says we could move closer to town, where the road is higher. I understand the attraction, especially for school and medical visits. But rent would be a new expense, and I would lose the customers and relatives who help us here. Staying is not simply refusing advice. Moving is not simply becoming safe. We need to compare the risks and the support we would lose in either place.

Interviewer — Q12: If residents could choose three changes, what would you prioritise?
Mere: First, I would choose reliable drinking water that everyone can reach. Second, I would arrange transport for people who need help leaving. Third, I would hold planning meetings when working residents can attend. I want our children to have choices rather than inherit only our repairs. We know how to help each other, but we should not have to solve every large problem with a collection of small household savings.

docs.name: 02_Bangladesh_Nasima_FICTIONAL.txt
docs.content:
FICTIONAL TRAINING INTERVIEW — NOT REAL RESEARCH DATA
Participant alias: Nasima
Setting: Fictional village in Patuakhali, Bangladesh
Interview language: English; scripted in English, not translated
All people, experiences, events and quotations below are invented.

Interviewer — Q1: Please tell me about your household and an ordinary day here.
Nasima: I sew clothes at home and grow vegetables when the soil allows it. My husband fishes, and my daughter helps her grandfather with his medicines after school. We do not have the same income every month, so we plan food and school costs carefully. I like living close to relatives. If a machine breaks or someone becomes ill, there is usually a person nearby who will come without being asked twice.

Interviewer — Q2: Describe a recent weather or environmental event that disrupted your life.
Nasima: In the event imagined for this interview, rain continued through the evening and water entered the yard before the strongest wind arrived. We put the sewing machine on a table and left for the shelter. When we returned, the floor was wet and salt marks remained on the vegetable beds. The house could be cleaned in a day, but the soil did not return to normal just because the water disappeared.

Interviewer — Q3: How did the event affect drinking water, sanitation, electricity or access to care?
Nasima: The nearby pond tasted salty after the flood, and the pump we usually used was surrounded by dirty water. I collected drinking water from a tank farther away. The queue was longer in the afternoon, so I went early and missed some sewing orders. Water was available somewhere, but getting it meant time, transport and somebody staying with my father. When people say the water problem is solved, I ask whose daily journey has become shorter.

Interviewer — Q4: What changed in your work, food supply, income or debts?
Nasima: My husband lost several fishing days and I could not use the machine until the room was dry. We bought vegetables that we normally grew and borrowed for school expenses. The lender knows us, which made borrowing easy, but the repayment still came before the next harvest. I accepted fewer orders because of the water trips. The flood connected our lost income to new household costs, rather than creating one separate bill.

Interviewer — Q5: How do you hear about danger, and how do you decide which information to trust?
Nasima: A volunteer announced the warning with a loudspeaker, and my daughter checked messages on her phone. I listened to both. The useful part was hearing when the shelter would open and which route was passable. Sometimes neighbours wait because earlier warnings did not lead to severe damage. I would rather receive an explanation of the uncertainty than a message that sounds completely certain and later seems wrong.

Interviewer — Q6: Tell me about deciding whether to leave or stay during an emergency.
Nasima: We left before dark because my father walks slowly. The shelter had space, but carrying his bedding and medicines was difficult. I worried about privacy and whether the toilets would be usable for him. A neighbour accompanied us, which helped. We were not choosing between a safe house and a dangerous shelter. We were choosing between different difficulties, and trying to make the least harmful choice with the information we had.

Interviewer — Q7: Who helped, and what did neighbours or community groups do?
Nasima: The women nearby shared cooking and took turns going for water. My niece watched the younger children while we cleaned the rooms. These arrangements were practical, not formal committees. One household had moved here recently and did not know whom to ask, so we invited them into the cooking group. Support becomes stronger when somebody notices who is missing, rather than assuming that every family already has relatives to rely on.

Interviewer — Q8: Did the disruption affect some people more than others?
Nasima: My daughter missed lessons while helping her grandfather, and I did unpaid care while trying to earn from sewing. My husband also worked hard, but his repair work was visible outside the house. Our extra work was inside. I want programmes to recognise both. If a household receives a water container, it still matters who fills it, who carries it, and who gives up paid work to make that possible.

Interviewer — Q9: What support did you receive, and how much say did residents have in decisions?
Nasima: We received food support, but the repair assistance required documents that had become wet. I visited the office twice and paid for transport both times. A staff member eventually helped me replace the papers. That kindness mattered, yet the process should not require finding a particularly helpful person. Residents should know the rules in advance and have a way to ask questions without losing several days of work.

Interviewer — Q10: What have you changed to prepare for the next disruption?
Nasima: We keep documents in a covered container and have changed part of the garden to crops we hope will tolerate the conditions better. I also keep the machine on a higher platform. These changes reduce some losses, but they cost money before we know whether they will work. We cannot raise the road ourselves. Household preparation and public maintenance need to support each other, or one blocked route can undo many careful preparations.

Interviewer — Q11: Have you considered moving away, temporarily or permanently?
Nasima: We have discussed renting a room near town for my daughter's studies, but moving the whole family would be much harder. My father wants to stay close to the people he knows. I do not want my daughter to feel she must give up education to look after everyone. A temporary move might help, although it would create two sets of expenses. For us, moving is a family negotiation rather than a single yes or no decision.

Interviewer — Q12: If residents could choose three changes, what would you prioritise?
Nasima: I would prioritise nearby drinking water, a shelter with toilets that older people can use, and assistance that does not disappear when documents are damaged. I would also ask officials to listen to the people who collect water and care for relatives. We can explain details that are missed in a quick visit. Fair support should reduce the work of recovery, not add another queue to an already crowded day.

docs.name: 03_Nepal_Arun_FICTIONAL.txt
docs.content:
FICTIONAL TRAINING INTERVIEW — NOT REAL RESEARCH DATA
Participant alias: Arun
Setting: Fictional hillside settlement in central Nepal, Nepal
Interview language: English; scripted in English, not translated
All people, experiences, events and quotations below are invented.

Interviewer — Q1: Please tell me about your household and an ordinary day here.
Arun: I farm a small plot with my wife and take construction work when it is available. Our son attends the school across the valley, and my aunt lives in the next house. Most mornings begin with checking the animals and the water pipe. The path between households is part of our daily life. We visit, share tools and carry produce along it, so a damaged path changes more than the journey to market.

Interviewer — Q2: Describe a recent weather or environmental event that disrupted your life.
Arun: During the heavy rain imagined in this interview, stones fell onto the path and a section of the slope slipped below the road. We heard the noise before we could see what had happened. Nobody in our household was injured, but we stayed with relatives that night because the ground beside the house felt uncertain. After the rain stopped, I still watched every new crack. The end of the storm did not immediately end the worry.

Interviewer — Q3: How did the event affect drinking water, sanitation, electricity or access to care?
Arun: The pipe from the spring broke where the slope moved. We walked to another tap and carried water back, while people tried to repair the connection. The clinic was on the other side of the damaged road, so my aunt postponed a check-up. A water repair and a road repair seem like separate tasks, but both decide whether someone can manage an ordinary day. Services need routes and people, not just equipment.

Interviewer — Q4: What changed in your work, food supply, income or debts?
Arun: We could not send vegetables to market while the road was blocked. Some spoiled before a vehicle could come, and I missed construction work that would have paid for school materials. A trader offered a lower price because he had to arrange extra transport. I accepted it because the produce could not wait. Our loss was not visible as a broken building; it was the income that never arrived and the choices that became narrower.

Interviewer — Q5: How do you hear about danger, and how do you decide which information to trust?
Arun: I heard the rain warning on the radio and from a message shared by a local teacher. The forecast covered a large area, so we also checked the slope and stream ourselves. I trust information more when it explains what to watch for locally. People with poor phone reception need another route for the warning. A map on a screen is useful, but somebody still has to turn it into a decision about this particular path.

Interviewer — Q6: Tell me about deciding whether to leave or stay during an emergency.
Arun: We decided to leave when small stones kept falling and the path became slippery. My aunt did not want to go because she feared leaving the animals. We arranged for a neighbour to check them and carried her bag to a relative's house. The temporary place was crowded but felt safer for that night. Planning should include where people can stay for several days, not only telling them to leave at the first sign of danger.

Interviewer — Q7: Who helped, and what did neighbours or community groups do?
Arun: Several neighbours cleared a walking route before any machine arrived. Others shared food and let children sleep in their houses. I joined the work, but people who were injured or caring for relatives could not contribute in the same way. They should not receive less help because of that. Community work is valuable when contributions can differ, rather than when every household must supply the same labour to be considered deserving.

Interviewer — Q8: Did the disruption affect some people more than others?
Arun: My wife carried water and looked after our son while I helped reopen the path. I received thanks at the community meeting, while her work was described as normal household duty. I noticed that difference after she pointed it out. A family may appear to recover quickly because somebody is absorbing more work in private. We should ask each person what changed, instead of treating the household as if it had only one experience.

Interviewer — Q9: What support did you receive, and how much say did residents have in decisions?
Arun: An officer visited and photographed the damaged road. We were told that larger repairs would depend on a later budget decision. Residents asked about the smaller path to the water point, but it was not included in that first discussion. I understand that resources are limited. Still, the route used daily by people carrying water should count alongside the road used by vehicles. We need a chance to explain our priorities before the plan is settled.

Interviewer — Q10: What have you changed to prepare for the next disruption?
Arun: We redirect some runoff away from the house and check the pipe before the rainy season. A few families are testing small retaining measures with local advice. I do not know enough to say that every wall is safe, so I would like skilled inspection rather than copying a neighbour's design. There is a limit to what unpaid work can repair. Preparation should include maintenance and advice that people can actually afford.

Interviewer — Q11: Have you considered moving away, temporarily or permanently?
Arun: My brother works in the city and says I could join him. Seasonal work away from home might help with the repair bills, but someone would still need to farm and care for our aunt. Moving permanently would mean losing our plot and support nearby. I am considering options rather than making a final decision. It matters whether a move is a choice that expands our future or a last response after every local option has failed.

Interviewer — Q12: If residents could choose three changes, what would you prioritise?
Arun: I would choose a reliable path to water and school, timely inspection of unstable ground, and support for households whose income stops when roads close. Residents should help decide which routes are repaired first. I want our son to understand the risks without growing up afraid of every rainfall. We can contribute knowledge and labour, but technical advice and dependable public support are also necessary.

docs.name: 04_Indonesia_Sari_FICTIONAL.txt
docs.content:
FICTIONAL TRAINING INTERVIEW — NOT REAL RESEARCH DATA
Participant alias: Sari
Setting: Fictional low-lying neighbourhood near Semarang, Indonesia
Interview language: English; scripted in English, not translated
All people, experiences, events and quotations below are invented.

Interviewer — Q1: Please tell me about your household and an ordinary day here.
Sari: I prepare breakfast food at home and sell it to workers on the morning shift. My husband does delivery jobs, and our nephew stays with us during school terms. We rent our house, so I cannot change every part of it. I value the customers who know my cooking and the neighbours who watch the stall when I step away. The neighbourhood is also a network that makes a small business possible.

Interviewer — Q2: Describe a recent weather or environmental event that disrupted your life.
Sari: In the flooding imagined for this interview, water entered the lane during the afternoon and rose again after heavy rain. I lifted the stove and food containers, but the doorway stayed wet for two days. Some neighbours said the water was routine, although this time it stayed longer. Calling a flood ordinary can hide the work it creates. We cleaned, waited, cleaned again, and tried to keep the business running between those tasks.

Interviewer — Q3: How did the event affect drinking water, sanitation, electricity or access to care?
Sari: We had to protect the drinking water containers from the dirty water in the lane. The electricity was interrupted, and I threw away some ingredients because the refrigerator could not keep them cool. Getting to the clinic meant using a longer route. My nephew helped carry containers, but he could not do that during school hours. Safe water was not only a question of supply; it was also storage, power and the route through the neighbourhood.

Interviewer — Q4: What changed in your work, food supply, income or debts?
Sari: Customers could not reach the stall and my husband had fewer delivery trips. I still owed rent, and I used the money set aside for supplies to pay it. Reopening meant buying ingredients before I had earned anything new. A neighbour lent me a small amount without interest, which helped. I want assistance to notice this gap between surviving the flood and being able to start earning again.

Interviewer — Q5: How do you hear about danger, and how do you decide which information to trust?
Sari: The neighbourhood group shared tide information and rain warnings on our phones. One neighbour printed the times and put them near the shop for people who were not in the group. I found that useful because messages disappear among many other conversations. We also needed to know when a route would become difficult. A warning becomes practical when it helps me decide when to move the stove and when to stop serving food.

Interviewer — Q6: Tell me about deciding whether to leave or stay during an emergency.
Sari: We did not leave immediately because the water was shallow inside and we feared losing the equipment. Later we stayed with a relative for one night. My landlord wanted to know whether we had damaged the floor, which added another worry. Tenants need a clear place in emergency planning. The person living in the house may be responsible for staying safe without having the authority or money to make the house safer.

Interviewer — Q7: Who helped, and what did neighbours or community groups do?
Sari: People in the lane lent raised shelves and shared a pump. We exchanged messages about open routes and checked on an older neighbour who lived alone. The support was quick because we knew one another. A delivery worker renting a room nearby was not in the phone group, so he learned about the route later. We added him after that. A neighbourhood network should be able to welcome people whose work keeps them away during meetings.

Interviewer — Q8: Did the disruption affect some people more than others?
Sari: I cleaned the cooking area before dawn, prepared less food, and then helped my nephew get to school by the longer route. My husband had his own work problems, but the cleaning and care tasks fell mostly to me. I was tired even on days when the stall did not open. People counted the lost sales, but nobody counted the extra hours needed to make the room usable again.

Interviewer — Q9: What support did you receive, and how much say did residents have in decisions?
Sari: Officials helped clear one drain, and that made a visible difference for part of the lane. I also asked about assistance for tenants, but I was told to speak to the property owner. The owner lived elsewhere and did not depend on the stall. I would like residents who rent to be heard directly. Support based only on ownership can overlook the people who are present during the flood and do the recovery work.

Interviewer — Q10: What have you changed to prepare for the next disruption?
Sari: I now store ingredients on higher shelves and keep a list of customers I can contact if the stall cannot open. Neighbours are trying a shared cleaning schedule for the drains. These changes help, but shelves do not stop water entering the lane. I cannot approve a major alteration to a rented house. We need coordination between residents, owners and public services, otherwise each person can do only a small part of the job.

Interviewer — Q11: Have you considered moving away, temporarily or permanently?
Sari: We have looked at rooms on higher ground, but the rent is higher and my customers would not follow me automatically. Staying keeps the business network, while moving could reduce some flooding. I do not feel there is a simple safe option. If help were available for restarting a small business elsewhere, moving would become more realistic. Advice to relocate should include a way to rebuild work and relationships, not just a new address.

Interviewer — Q12: If residents could choose three changes, what would you prioritise?
Sari: My priorities are drainage that is maintained, support that includes tenants, and small-business assistance that arrives before another rent payment is due. Meetings should include the people who work early mornings or late evenings. I want a neighbourhood where we prepare together but do not accept endless cleaning as normal. We should be able to earn, rest and send children to school without organising every ordinary day around the next flood.

codes.definition: Hopes for education, choice, rest, safety or fair future conditions.

Raising the whole house would cost much more than we earn. I also worry that a stronger wall at one property could send water towards another. Preparation should look at the whole neighbourhood, not just at the safest single house.

We need to compare the risks and the support we would lose in either place.

I sew clothes at home and grow vegetables when the soil allows it. My husband fishes, and my daughter helps her grandfather with his medicines after school. We do not have the same income every month, so we plan food and school costs carefully. I like living close to relatives. If a machine breaks or someone becomes ill, there is usually a person nearby who will come without being asked twice.

The nearby pond tasted salty after the flood, and the pump we usually used was surrounded by dirty water. I collected drinking water from a tank farther away. The queue was longer in the afternoon, so I went early and missed some sewing orders. Water was available somewhere, but getting it meant time, transport and somebody staying with my father. When people say the water problem is solved, I ask whose daily journey has become shorter.

The flood connected our lost income to new household costs, rather than creating one separate bill.

A volunteer announced the warning with a loudspeaker, and my daughter checked messages on her phone. I listened to both. The useful part was hearing when the shelter would open and which route was passable. Sometimes neighbours wait because earlier warnings did not lead to severe damage. I would rather receive an explanation of the uncertainty than a message that sounds completely certain and later seems wrong.

We left before dark because my father walks slowly. The shelter had space, but carrying his bedding and medicines was difficult. I worried about privacy and whether the toilets would be usable for him. A neighbour accompanied us, which helped. We were not choosing between a safe house and a dangerous shelter. We were choosing between different difficulties, and trying to make the least harmful choice with the information we had.

Support becomes stronger when somebody notices who is missing, rather than assuming that every family already has relatives to rely on.

Fair support should reduce the work of recovery, not add another queue to an already crowded day.

I farm a small plot with my wife and take construction work when it is available. Our son attends the school across the valley, and my aunt lives in the next house. Most mornings begin with checking the animals and the water pipe. The path between households is part of our daily life. We visit, share tools and carry produce along it, so a damaged path changes more than the journey to market.

The pipe from the spring broke where the slope moved. We walked to another tap and carried water back, while people tried to repair the connection. The clinic was on the other side of the damaged road, so my aunt postponed a check-up. A water repair and a road repair seem like separate tasks, but both decide whether someone can manage an ordinary day. Services need routes and people, not just equipment.

Our loss was not visible as a broken building; it was the income that never arrived and the choices that became narrower.

I heard the rain warning on the radio and from a message shared by a local teacher. The forecast covered a large area, so we also checked the slope and stream ourselves. I trust information more when it explains what to watch for locally. People with poor phone reception need another route for the warning. A map on a screen is useful, but somebody still has to turn it into a decision about this particular path.

We decided to leave when small stones kept falling and the path became slippery. My aunt did not want to go because she feared leaving the animals. We arranged for a neighbour to check them and carried her bag to a relative's house. The temporary place was crowded but felt safer for that night. Planning should include where people can stay for several days, not only telling them to leave at the first sign of danger.

Community work is valuable when contributions can differ, rather than when every household must supply the same labour to be considered deserving.

We rent our house, so I cannot change every part of it. I value the customers who know my cooking and the neighbours who watch the stall when I step away. The neighbourhood is also a network that makes a small business possible.

A warning becomes practical when it helps me decide when to move the stove and when to stop serving food.

The person living in the house may be responsible for staying safe without having the authority or money to make the house safer.
